chaos_scenario.title: Migrating to the New Architecture Under Load...

steps.label: Thundering herd of HTTP polling eliminated
Full table scans replaced by O(1) Geo queries
Stripe API timeout absorbed by message queues

levels.title: Level 1: Escaping the Monolithic Bottleneck
levels.description: The legacy system consists of a single server and mobile apps that constantly poll via HTTP. Fix the ingress layer to prevent connection exhaustion and SPOFs.

questions.text: Flaw: The mobile app connects directly to a single IP address of one monolithic server. If it crashes, the business stops. How do you resolve this Single Point of Failure (SPOF)?
choices: Hardcode three different IPs in the mobile app code
Introduce a Global Load Balancer pointing to an API Gateway backed by an auto-scaling group
Move the monolith to a larger mainframe server
questions.correct_answer: Introduce a Global Load Balancer pointing to an API Gateway backed by an auto-scaling group
questions.explanation: A Global Load Balancer removes the SPOF at ingress, dynamically routing traffic to healthy instances in an auto-scaling group via an API Gateway.
questions.uml_mutation:
client((Mobile Apps)) --> glb[Global Load Balancer]
    glb --> api[API Gateway]

questions.text: Flaw: 100,000 drivers send GPS updates via HTTP POST every 3 seconds. The TLS handshake overhead is melting the server CPU (Thundering Herd). What protocol fixes this?
choices: HTTP/1.0
Persistent WebSockets
FTP (File Transfer Protocol)
questions.explanation: WebSockets maintain a long-lived, persistent, bi-directional TCP connection. This entirely eliminates the CPU-intensive HTTP handshake overhead for high-frequency location streaming.

questions.text: Flaw: The monolith tries to process, validate, and write every GPS ping synchronously. During traffic spikes, the server locks up. How do we safely buffer this massive write-heavy ingestion?
choices: Write location logs to local CSV files
Drop 50% of the location packets randomly
Publish the pings to a high-throughput event stream (like Apache Kafka)
questions.correct_answer: Publish the pings to a high-throughput event stream (like Apache Kafka)
questions.explanation: Kafka acts as a highly durable shock absorber. It decouples the fast ingestion of GPS data from the slower downstream processing services, preventing system overload.

levels.title: Level 2: Fixing the Database Meltdown
levels.description: The legacy system uses a single MySQL database for everything. Queries are locking, and spatial lookups are timing out.

questions.text: Flaw: Finding a nearby driver involves a SQL query: `SELECT * FROM drivers WHERE lat BETWEEN X AND Y`. This triggers a full table scan taking seconds. What is the modern fix?
choices: Add more RAM to the MySQL server
Implement an in-memory Geospatial Database (like Redis Geo / Geohash)
Fetch all drivers to the mobile app and calculate distance on the phone
questions.correct_answer: Implement an in-memory Geospatial Database (like Redis Geo / Geohash)
questions.explanation: Redis Geo uses Geohashes to map 2D coordinates into 1D strings, allowing spatial lookups (finding nearby drivers) to execute in O(log N) time entirely in memory.
questions.uml_mutation:
kafka --> locSvc[Location Service]
    locSvc --> redisGeo[(Redis Geospatial Index)]

questions.text: Flaw: Every time a user opens the app, the system queries the DB for their static profile and settings, starving the DB of connections. How do we offload these reads?
choices: Introduce a Distributed Cache (Redis/Memcached) for read-heavy static data
Store all profiles in Kafka
Switch the database to SQLite
questions.correct_answer: Introduce a Distributed Cache (Redis/Memcached) for read-heavy static data
questions.explanation: A distributed cache sits in front of the database (Cache-Aside pattern), serving frequent read requests in sub-milliseconds and freeing up database connections.
questions.uml_mutation:
api --> userSvc[User Service]
    userSvc --> cache[(Redis Distributed Cache)]

questions.text: Flaw: We still have a single primary relational database. If the hardware fails, data is lost and the system crashes. How do we add redundancy and further scale reads?
choices: Back up the database to an external hard drive every Sunday
Implement a Primary-Replica architecture with asynchronous replication
Run two active primary databases sharing the same disk
questions.correct_answer: Implement a Primary-Replica architecture with asynchronous replication
questions.explanation: A Primary-Replica setup ensures that if the primary dies, a replica can be promoted to prevent downtime. It also allows you to route heavy read queries exclusively to the replicas.
questions.uml_mutation:
userSvc --> dbPrimary[(SQL Primary DB)]
    dbPrimary -.->|Async Replication| dbReplica[(SQL Read Replicas)]
    userSvc --> dbReplica

levels.title: Level 3: Breaking Synchronous Traps & Scaling Writes
levels.description: Synchronous 3rd-party API calls are blocking threads, and historical data is maxing out the storage limits.

questions.text: Flaw: At the end of a ride, the monolith calls Stripe synchronously. If Stripe is slow, the driver's app hangs on 'Processing...' and server threads are blocked. How do we fix this?
choices: Reduce the HTTP timeout to 10 milliseconds
Decouple it using a Message Queue and an Asynchronous Payment Worker
Charge the user directly from their mobile phone
questions.correct_answer: Decouple it using a Message Queue and an Asynchronous Payment Worker
questions.explanation: By pushing a 'charge_request' to a message queue, the API can immediately respond 'Success' to the driver. The Payment Worker safely handles the charge in the background without blocking.
questions.uml_mutation:
api --> tripSvc[Trip Service]
    tripSvc --> payQueue[[Payment Queue]]
    payQueue --> payWorker[Async Payment Worker]

questions.text: Flaw: The legacy `trip_history` SQL table has 2 billion rows. Indexes no longer fit in RAM, and inserts are crawling. What is the best storage solution for immutable, high-volume historical logs?
choices: A horizontally scalable NoSQL wide-column store (like Cassandra)
Delete all trips older than 30 days
Move it to a Redis Cache
questions.correct_answer: A horizontally scalable NoSQL wide-column store (like Cassandra)
questions.explanation: Cassandra is designed for massive, append-heavy workloads. By partitioning historical trip data by UserID across many nodes, it provides infinite horizontal write scaling.

questions.text: Flaw: The legacy system relies on MySQL's AUTO_INCREMENT for Trip IDs. At 10,000 trips/second, this centralized lock creates a massive bottleneck. What pattern replaces this?
choices: Generate UUIDs in the database using a stored procedure
Use a Distributed ID Generator (like Twitter Snowflake / Ticket Server)
Use the timestamp as the ID
questions.correct_answer: Use a Distributed ID Generator (like Twitter Snowflake / Ticket Server)
questions.explanation: Snowflake algorithms generate highly unique, time-sortable 64-bit IDs locally across distributed workers without requiring a central database lock, entirely removing the write bottleneck.

levels.title: Level 4: Surviving Chaos & Scale
levels.description: The architecture is modernized, but we need safeguards against bad actors, cascading failures, and operational blind spots.

questions.text: Flaw: Competitors deploy botnets to rapidly request price estimates, trying to reverse-engineer our surge pricing. This DDOS attack exhausts our servers. Where do we stop this?
choices: At the Edge layer using a WAF and Rate Limiter before the API Gateway
By writing an if-statement in the Trip Service
By shutting down the Location Service
questions.correct_answer: At the Edge layer using a WAF and Rate Limiter before the API Gateway
questions.explanation: A Web Application Firewall (WAF) and Rate Limiter drop malicious or excessively repetitive traffic at the absolute edge of the network, before it consumes any internal compute resources.
questions.uml_mutation:
glb --> waf[WAF & Rate Limiter]
    waf --> api

questions.text: Flaw: When a payment fails due to insufficient funds, the Payment Worker instantly retries in a tight infinite loop, crashing the worker pool. What pattern handles failures gracefully?
choices: Ignore the error and assume it worked
A Dead Letter Queue (DLQ) paired with Exponential Backoff retries
Restart the Payment Worker automatically
questions.correct_answer: A Dead Letter Queue (DLQ) paired with Exponential Backoff retries
questions.explanation: Messages that fail processing are routed to a DLQ. Exponential backoff ensures retries happen at increasing intervals (1s, 2s, 4s), giving external services time to recover without overwhelming them.
questions.uml_mutation:
payWorker --> dlq[[Dead Letter Queue]]
    dlq -.->|Exponential Backoff| payWorker

questions.text: Flaw: A user complains that booking a trip took 15 seconds. With 20 different microservices, developers have no idea which service caused the delay. What resolves this operational blind spot?
choices: Distributed Tracing (e.g., Jaeger / OpenTelemetry) passing a Correlation ID
Reading the local text logs on all 500 servers
Adding `console.log('here')` in the code
questions.correct_answer: Distributed Tracing (e.g., Jaeger / OpenTelemetry) passing a Correlation ID
questions.explanation: Distributed tracing injects a unique Correlation ID at the API Gateway. This ID is passed between all microservices, allowing engineers to visualize the exact latency path and pinpoint the bottleneck.
questions.uml_mutation:
api -.-> obs[Distributed Tracing & Metrics]
    tripSvc -.-> obs
    userSvc -.-> obs
    style redisGeo fill:#065f46,stroke:#34d399
    style kafka fill:#065f46,stroke:#34d399
